passage: The school art exhibition was a week away, and every Class 9 student had to submit one drawing. Lokesh had no colours at home and only the lunch break to work in the crowded art room. He sketched a banyan tree, looked at Baljeet's page beside him, where a whole market scene was coming alive, and crumpled his paper. "I'm just not the creative type," he said. "Some people have it. I don't." Baljeet offered a spare pencil and said the tree trunk looked good. Lokesh shook his head. "Doesn't matter. I'll never be good at this." For the rest of the week he spent lunch in the canteen. On exhibition day his slot on the wall was empty, and he acted as if he didn't care.

qa.q: What did Lokesh sketch before crumpling the paper?
qa.a: A banyan tree.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh crumple his drawing after looking at Baljeet's page?
qa.a: Comparing his tree with Baljeet's market scene made him feel drawing is a gift he was born without, so trying seemed pointless and a bit humiliating.

qa.q: What could Lokesh have tried instead of giving up?
qa.a: Finishing the tree using Baljeet's spare pencil and the praise for the trunk, treating it as a starting level rather than a verdict.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel seeing the empty slot on the wall?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel sad and a little helpless, having offered a pencil and real praise that Lokesh wouldn't accept.

grounding: A teenager who struggles with drawing decides he lacks creativity and stops, leaving his exhibition slot empty.

passage: Asif stood at the back of the Sunday sketching class in Mylapore, looking at his page. The temple gopuram he'd drawn leaned as if about to fall. "I'm just not creative," he told Karthik. "My hands don't do it." Karthik showed him his own sketchbook from last year: wobbly lines, a lopsided cow. "This was me in June." Asif glanced at it and shrugged. "You're different. You have it. I don't." The instructor suggested he try the gopuram again, one tier at a time. Asif closed his book. "No point." The next Sunday he didn't come. Karthik sent him a photo of the gopuram, drawn tier by tier. Asif left it unread.

qa.q: What did Karthik show Asif from last year?
qa.a: His own sketchbook: wobbly lines, a lopsided cow.

qa.q: Why did Asif shrug off Karthik's old sketchbook?
qa.a: Asif felt discouraged; believing drawing ability is something you either have or don't, he read Karthik's improvement as proof that Karthik was just different.

qa.q: What turning point did Asif miss, and what might have helped?
qa.a: The instructor's suggestion to redraw one tier at a time; trying it would have shown him his own drawing could improve.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when the photo stays unread?
qa.a: Karthik may feel disappointed and shut out, having shared his own clumsy start to encourage a friend who won't listen.

grounding: A teenager decides he is simply not creative and quits sketching, turning his current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
"Shalini, where's your art project? It's due Monday."
"I'm not doing it, Amma."
Kavitha put down the vegetable knife. "Not doing it?"
"I can't draw. Everyone knows. Nithya draws like a real artist, and mine look like a baby's."
"You drew that beautiful kolam at Pongal."
"That's different. That's patterns. I'm not creative." Shalini pushed the sketchbook under the sofa. "Some people are born with it."
"Were you born reading?"
"What?"
"You couldn't read at three. Now you read my office letters for me."
Shalini frowned. "That's not the same."
"Maybe. Or maybe you're at the start of drawing, like you were once at the start of reading."
Shalini didn't answer, but she didn't push the sketchbook any further under, either.

qa.q: When is Shalini's art project due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: Why does Shalini say "Some people are born with it"?
qa.a: Shalini feels embarrassed next to Nithya, whose drawings look like a real artist's, and believing talent is inborn spares her from trying and failing.

qa.q: Which question from Kavitha might shift Shalini's view, and why?
qa.a: "Were you born reading?", because it reminds her of a skill she clearly built over time, suggesting drawing could grow too.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see her daughter's refusal?
qa.a: Kavitha doesn't accept "I'm not creative"; she sees a beginner, points to the kolam and to reading, and hopes Shalini will try.

grounding: A teenager decides she is not creative and stops, and her mother challenges the idea that talent is fixed.

passage: Last year I quit the drawing club after two weeks, and I told everyone the same thing: "I'm just not a creative person." I'm Yusuf. Our first exercise was drawing a hand, and mine looked like a bunch of bananas. Abhinav, next to me, drew one that looked real, with wrinkles on the knuckles. I remember thinking, some people have it and some don't, so why waste Saturdays? It felt like a fact, like being tall. This summer Abhinav showed me his old sketchbook from Class 6. His hands looked like bananas too. Worse than mine, honestly. He'd just kept going for three years. I haven't gone back to the club yet. But I've stopped saying "I'm not creative." Now I say, "I'm not good at hands yet."

qa.q: What did Yusuf's first drawing of a hand look like?
qa.a: It looked like a bunch of bananas.

qa.q: Why did quitting feel sensible to Yusuf at the time?
qa.a: Yusuf felt embarrassed and discouraged next to Abhinav's real-looking hand; talent seemed fixed, 'like being tall', so more Saturdays seemed a waste.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yusuf, and what did it change?
qa.a: Seeing Abhinav's Class 6 sketchbook full of banana hands; Yusuf stopped saying 'I'm not creative' and started saying 'not good at hands yet'.

qa.q: Why might Abhinav have shown Yusuf the old sketchbook?
qa.a: Abhinav may have noticed Yusuf giving up and wanted to show that his own skill came from three years of practice, not a gift.

grounding: A teenager who drew poorly decided to be 'just not creative' and quit, turning a current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
Art teacher's note, Class 9, 8 February. Irawati.
Sarika has stopped handing in drawings. When I asked, she said, "I'm just not creative, Ma'am. Some people are born artists. I'm not." Her first portrait this term was stiff, and she compared it with Rinchen's, which is very good. Since then she has handed in blank sheets with only her name on them. What worries me is that she's turning where she is now into where she'll always be. Today I showed her three of my own drawings from college, clumsy ones, and asked for one ten-minute sketch of her shoe, nothing else. She did it, grumbling. The laces were good, and I told her exactly what was good about them. Next week: the shoe again, from a different angle.

qa.q: What has Sarika handed in since the first portrait?
qa.a: Blank sheets with only her name on them.

qa.q: What does Sarika believe about talent when she says 'Some people are born artists'?
qa.a: Sarika feels discouraged and resigned, believing talent is fixed, so her stiff first portrait feels like a permanent verdict and trying again seems pointless.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati make today, and why might it help?
qa.a: Showing her own clumsy college drawings and asking for one ten-minute shoe sketch; a small task plus specific praise for the laces shows that skill can grow.

qa.q: What worries Irawati most about Sarika's words?
qa.a: Irawati worries that Sarika is turning her current level into a lifelong limit, and seems to care more about that belief than about any one missing drawing.

grounding: An art teacher sees a teenager decide she is just not creative and stop, and responds with a small task and specific praise.

passage:
Tuesday

Art period again. We had to draw a still life: a jug, two onions, a cloth. Mine looked like a potato next to a lamp post. Tanvir's looked like a photo. Everyone crowded round his.

I erased mine three times, and then I just stopped. I wrote "not creative" at the bottom in tiny letters and closed the book.

Some people are born with it. Tanvir draws on every notebook margin and has since Class 3. Me, I'm a numbers person. It's fine. That's just how brains work.

Sir said it takes practice. Easy for him to say, he's an artist.

I'm dropping the art elective next term. No point wasting time on something I can't do.

— Farhan

qa.q: Why does dropping the art elective feel sensible to Farhan?

passage: The art room of the government girls' school in Sagar had one fan and thirty easels. Hemant sir asked the Class 9 students to draw the banyan tree outside the window. Sunaina tried. The trunk was too thin; the branches looked like sticks. The girl next to her had drawn every hanging root. Sunaina put down her pencil. "I'm just not creative, sir. Some people are born with it." Hemant sir said, "Your first try is where you start, not where you finish." She nodded politely, but after that, in every art class, she sat at the back doing her maths homework. When the annual exhibition came, Sunaina's section on the wall was empty. She walked past it quickly, telling herself it didn't matter.

qa.q: What did Hemant sir ask the students to draw?
qa.a: The banyan tree outside the window.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina walk past the empty section quickly?
qa.a: She felt a bit embarrassed and hurt, though she told herself it didn't matter, because believing she wasn't creative had stopped her from trying.

qa.q: What might help Sunaina keep trying at art?
qa.a: Starting with small, regular sketches of the tree and comparing them over weeks, as Hemant sir suggested, could show her that skill grows.

qa.q: How might Hemant sir see Sunaina's move to the back of the class?
qa.a: Hemant sir might feel disappointed and concerned, seeing her give up after one try.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is weak at drawing and says she's not creative, turning her current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
Mei had always drawn a little in the margins of her notes, at her school in Singapore. In Year 10 art, the first project was a portrait. Hers looked flat, with the eyes too far apart.
Her classmate Noa's portrait looked almost like a photograph.
Mei put her pencil down. “I'm just not creative. Some people have it, some don't.”
“I've been drawing every day since I was ten,” Noa said. “My first faces looked like potatoes.”
“That's different. You're naturally good.”
The next week Mei chose the written option instead of the art project. When the art teacher asked why, she said, “I'm not an art person.”
She stopped drawing in her margins too. The notebook pages stayed clean and white.

qa.q: What was the first Year 10 art project?
qa.a: A portrait.

qa.q: Why did Mei put her pencil down after seeing Noa's portrait?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and inadequate, believing creativity is fixed and she simply doesn't have it.

qa.q: What could the art teacher say to help Mei?
qa.a: The teacher could show how skills like spacing the eyes can be learned step by step, and invite her to practise one small thing.

qa.q: How does Noa see the portrait skill?
qa.a: Noa sees that skill as the result of years of daily practice, starting from faces that looked like potatoes.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager deciding she is just not creative after one weak portrait, turning her current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
In the art room of the Kanpur girls' school, Sonali Ma'am handed back the still-life sketches. Rukmini, fifteen, looked at hers: a lopsided jug, wobbly shadows.
“I'm just not creative, Ma'am. Some people are born with it.”
“Rukmini, this is your third sketch ever.”
“And it's bad.”
“It's early.”
Rukmini shook her head. “My sister's an artist. She got all the talent. I got maths.” She pushed the sketch into her bag, crumpled.
For the rest of term, she chose the easiest tasks: tracing, colouring inside printed lines. When they had to draw from life again, she said she had a headache.
Sonali Ma'am watched her, frowning. She'd seen Rukmini's first sketch and her third side by side. The third was better. Rukmini just hadn't looked.

qa.q: What did Rukmini sketch?
qa.a: She sketched a still life with a jug.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini crumple her sketch into her bag?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged, believing talent is fixed and that her sister got it all.

qa.q: What could Sonali Ma'am do next to help Rukmini?
qa.a: Show Rukmini her first and third sketches side by side, so she can see she is already improving.

qa.q: How does Sonali Ma'am see Rukmini's drawing?
qa.a: Sonali Ma'am sees real improvement from the first sketch to the third and feels concerned that Rukmini hasn't noticed.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager who is weak at drawing deciding she is not creative and avoiding it, turning her current level into a fixed limit.

passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,

You asked why I dropped the art elective. The truth is, I'm just not a creative person. You got those genes, not me.

On the first day we had to draw a hand. Everyone else's looked like a hand. Mine looked like a glove full of sticks. The teacher said it was “a start.” I knew what that meant.

So I switched to accountancy. I'm good with numbers. That's who I am.

Sometimes, though, in accountancy class, I doodle little birds in the corner of the page. They're not very good. I cross them out before anyone sees.

Anyway, how's your exhibition going? Send me pictures.

Rajni

qa.a: Rajni seems to still enjoy drawing but feels embarrassed and inadequate, believing creativity is a fixed trait Rajni lacks.

passage:
Before: In September, Gautam and his friend Raghav both joined the Saturday sketching club at their school. Gautam's first portrait came out lopsided. He laughed it off.
During: In October, the teacher pinned all the portraits on the corridor board for the parents' day. A group of juniors stopped at Gautam's and giggled. That evening he told his mother, "I'm not a creative person. I'm a maths person. Some people just have it." He didn't go to the club the next Saturday, or the one after.
After: In February, Gautam walked past the corridor board again. Raghav's new portrait hung there, a shaded face with real eyes. Raghav had also been bad in September. Gautam stopped for a second, then walked on quickly. "He's just talented," he muttered. "I'm not."

qa.q: What did the juniors do at Gautam's portrait?
qa.a: They stopped and giggled.

qa.q: Why does Gautam walk away quickly from Raghav's portrait?
qa.a: He feels uncomfortable and a bit envious, and telling himself Raghav is just talented protects him from seeing that practice made the difference.

qa.q: What could help Gautam rethink his belief?
qa.a: Comparing Raghav's September sketch with the February one could show him that skill grew with practice, and he could try one Saturday session again.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Gautam's claim that he is "just talented"?
qa.a: Raghav might feel frustrated or unseen, since he knows he was also bad in September and improved through months of practice.

grounding: It shows a teenager who was weak at drawing deciding he is just not creative and stopping, turning his current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
"Tanuja, you think you can't paint because you tried once? Listen to your Pallavi masi's story.
When I was fourteen, our drawing teacher asked us to paint a village scene. My huts leaned, my cows looked like dogs, and my river was brown. The girl next to me had painted a sunset so beautiful that the teacher showed it to the principal.
That day I decided: some people are artists. I'm not. I put my colour box under the bed and never took it out again.
For twenty-three years I said, 'I'm not creative,' as if it were my blood group.
Last year, when your cousin joined a weekend art class, I sat at the back to wait for her. The teacher handed me paper. My first drawing was terrible. My tenth was not bad. My thirtieth, I framed.
I wasn't uncreative. I just stopped at fourteen."

qa.q: How long did Pallavi say "I'm not creative"?
qa.a: She said it for twenty-three years.

qa.q: How did young Pallavi feel after seeing the sunset painting next to hers?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and small, deciding that some people are artists and she was not.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pallavi masi's story?
qa.a: Sitting at the back of the weekend art class, she was handed paper and kept drawing; by her thirtieth drawing she saw that practice, not fixed talent, made the difference.

qa.q: How might the girl who painted the sunset have seen young Pallavi's decision?
qa.a: That girl may not have known her painting made Pallavi quit, and might have been surprised that one comparison shaped so many years.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a teenager who was weak at painting deciding she was not creative and stopping, which turned her level at fourteen into a long limit.

passage:
The art portfolio was due the Monday after Holi, and Yash had three days left, most of them booked for his cousin's wedding. Friday evening he sat on the balcony with a pencil, trying to draw the neem tree. The trunk came out like a pipe. He erased it twice and tore the paper.
Gopika, his sister, still had pink colour on her ears from the morning. "Want me to show you the shading trick?"
"No point. Some people are just born artists. I'm not creative. I'll take the zero." He put the pencil back in the box and snapped it shut.
"You've drawn for, what, twenty minutes this year?"
"That's what I'm saying. It's not in me." He went inside and switched on the cricket. The blank page stayed on the balcony chair, curling in the heat.

qa.q: What was Yash trying to draw on the balcony?
qa.a: He was trying to draw the neem tree.

qa.q: Why does giving up feel reasonable to Yash?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and a little embarrassed, and telling himself he is just not creative makes quitting feel like accepting a fact instead of failing.

qa.q: What would you advise Yash with the deadline so close?
qa.a: He could accept Gopika's shading trick and aim to finish one small, rough drawing, treating it as practice rather than proof of talent.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel when Yash turns down her help?
qa.a: Gopika may feel brushed off and a bit sad, since she can see he has hardly practised and is giving up far too early.

grounding: A teenager who draws poorly decides he is simply not creative and stops, turning his current level into a fixed limit.
